title: They ate, your honor 🍽️  Hungry Women is now playing at SoHo Playhous...
transcript: In 1831, all of the men in the world suddenly perished. That is the jumping off point for the new play, Hungry Women. And what begins as a simple moral discussion around if the wives should eat their now deceased husbands eventually evolves into something much larger, giving us a look into this woman only society, examining what this society would look like and if it would actually be the Utopia that it seems on paper. This play has so many twists and turns and you never quite know where it's going to go next. It is told in three distinct parts, each introducing us to four new characters. But without spoiling too much, they do build off each other in very interesting ways. And it's the show's ability to constantly reinvent itself that I think is one of its biggest strengths. Just when you think it has explored everything it can with a given premise, it suddenly shapeshifts into something completely new. But the other reason to see the show is Julia Lester, who is very quickly becoming one of my favorite actresses working today. She is consistently so excellent in every single thing that she does and continues to be here. This is very much an ensemble show, but I think Julia really stands above the rest, playing three characters that feel so fully formed and so distinct from one another. I will never miss a Julia Lester performance, and neither should you! it's easy to see Why this play won the Lighthouse Series, which is a playwriting competition hosted by Soho Playhouse. It is funny and fresh and wholly unique, so I'm really glad they've now had the opportunity to bring it back and give it the full staging that it deserves. It does still feel a bit held back due to the limitations of the space, and I hope that they're able to continue to grow the production. And so Hungry Women is going to be a Broadway Ben recommendation.
classificationReason: Creator reviews Hungry Women at SoHo Playhouse with clear first-hand opinions on structure, pacing, and Julia Lester's standout performance. Presents personal assessment of the production's strengths.
